entry.title: Shrink Your Docker Image by 60% Using Multi-Stage Builds and Distroless Containers
entry.summary:
Hey Devs! 👋
I’m Anusha, the voice behind Data Enthusiast Era — a channel where I simplify DevOps, Data Science, and MLOps, especially for folks getting started. Recently, I managed to reduce a Docker image from 146MB to just 57MB.
No tricks. Just Multi-Stage Docker Builds and Distroless Containers.
Here’s how I did it — explained in a way that actually makes sense if you're new to Docker or DevOps. When we use official base images like python:3.11 or node, they include: a shell compilers package managers other stuff you don’t need at runtime
This makes the image: Bigger Slower to deploy More vulnerable With Multi-Stage Builds, we split the Dockerfile into two parts: One for building (with all tools needed) One for running (with only the app and its dependencies) It’s like packing light for production — just what you need to survive! Distroless images are minimal base images built by Google.
They don’t include: /bin/bash a shell any package manager Which means: ✨ Smaller 🔐 More secure ⚡ Faster to run FROM python:3.11-slim WORKDIR /app COPY requirements.txt . RUN pip install -r requirements.txt COPY . . CMD ["python", "main.py"]
🛑 Image size: 146MB Step 2: Multi-Stage + Distroless FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder WORKDIR /app COPY requirements.txt . RUN pip install --target=/install -r requirements.txt COPY . .
FROM gcr.io/distroless/python3 COPY --from=builder /install /usr/local/lib/python3.11/site-packages COPY --from=builder /app /app WORKDIR /app CMD ["main.py"]
✅ Image size: 57.8MB 📊 Result: 🎉 That’s a 60% image size reduction — in production, that’s a huge win. 🔍 Why This Matters 🔐 Reduce attack surface 🧹 Avoid leftover tools and clutter 💸 Save cloud storage and bandwidth 🎥 Watch the Full Demo 🙌 Final Thoughts I’m Anusha Kuppili — a woman in tech and the creator of Data Enthusiast Era, where I make tech concepts simple, visual, and fun to learn. Let me know in the comments: 💡 Follow me on: https://www.youtube.com/@DataEnthusiastEra

entry.title: nullptr in C23
entry.summary:
Introduction
Since its creation in the 1970s, C has used the preprocessor to define a macro for the “null pointer.” Originally, it was defined as: #define NULL 0
or perhaps 0L since void and the ability to use void* weren’t added until C89. This required C to have a special case for the integer literals 0 and 0L (and 0LL once long long was added in C99, as well as their unsigned variants) allowing only them to be converted to any pointer type implicitly: char *p = 0; // OK char *q = 1; // error
For simplicity, going forward, whenever I mention 0 as a possible definition of NULL, interpret that to mean either 0 or any one of 0U, 0L, 0UL, 0LL, or 0ULL. Since C89, NULL is typically instead defined as: #define NULL ((void*)0)
which is better; however, some platforms still define it …
